name: Felix Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Felix, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Felix, 27, and I live with my girlfriend Ama, who's a nurse on a children's ward. I left school early because I wanted money more than exams, and I've done delivery driving, a bit of labouring, and now about a year and a half in the warehouse. We rent a two-bed and split everything down the middle. I've got around eight months of bills saved, which my dad says is more than he ever had at my age.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on days at the warehouse of an online clothes shop, seven till half three. I get a handheld that sends me to a shelf, I grab the jumper or the trainers, scan, drop it in a plastic tote, and the tote goes onto a conveyor to the packing benches. Some days I'm on returns, which is opening bags people sent back and checking for make-up on collars. I'm still not quick, and I lose time when the shelf numbers jump about. I like the lads on my aisle and the walking, I do about 20,000 steps. What I don't like is the music being the same twelve songs on repeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So all the talk was mostly noise. Fair enough, I wouldn't be shocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like: see, people still need hands. I'd probably post a meme about it in the group chat with the lads from five-a-side. At work I'd say the managers spent a lot of money on screens for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think good, because my job stays my job. I use a chatbot now and then for things like writing to my landlord, and that's handy, but I don't need it to change my life. If it's just that, I keep my wage and my savings keep going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep putting about 300 a month into savings. I'd probably do the forklift licence at some point, because it's a bit more per hour and the trainer, Kwame, keeps nagging me. Nothing big, no panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd even feel a bit smug, if I'm honest. I don't like being told the world's ending every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine bit of your day that a small bit of AI could take over in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the returns checking. They've got a camera that looks at clothes and says if they're damaged, it's being tried on one bench. If it works, they'd need fewer of us on returns. But there's always picking to move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ama think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama laughs at me for worrying, because nobody's replacing a nurse on a kids' ward. She says I should do a course anyway, just because. She's right, but I always say next year.

say: I'd tell the group chat that **people still need hands**, maybe with a meme.
I'd say at work the managers wasted **money on screens** that changed little.
think: My **job stays my job**, and that's a relief.
A chatbot is **handy** for letters, but I don't need it to change my life.
do: Keep doing day shifts and save about **300 a month**.
Take the **forklift licence** at some point, since it pays a bit more per hour.
feel: **Calm**, even a bit **smug** about the hype fading.
Tired of hearing the **world's ending** every week.
S0.quote: I don't like being told the world's ending every week.
fieldNote: Secure **savings** and a partner in **nursing** keep the household steady.
He notices the **returns camera** trial, but sees picking as a fallback.
He puts off a **course** year after year, a sign of comfortable inertia.

steps.text: Keep working day shifts and save about 300 a month
Book the forklift licence course with the warehouse trainer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one sounds closer to what's actually happening. The office people already use AI for the stock orders, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say: it's the office first, then us, so let's get organised before it's our turn. I'm in the union but I'm not a rep, I'd probably go to more meetings. Online I'd share stuff about making companies pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my picking job is all right for a few years, because shelves and jumpers are fiddly for robots. But I'd see fewer new hires and more pressure on the rate, because the software planning the shifts would cut slack. My worry is that 'some time to adjust' turns into 'adjust by next month'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence this year, no more next year. I'd try the AI stuff the office uses if they offered it, once I'd seen a few others get on with it. And I'd keep the savings where they are, not touch them, maybe add a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for me exactly, more like watching the tide come in and knowing it'll reach my bit eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Jordan, who does the scheduling for the vans going out. He's clever but it's all spreadsheets and phone calls. That's exactly the kind of thing the card says AI takes, and he's got a little boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd wait till others try the AI tools first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half the new things they bring in get dropped after three months. Remember the voice-picking headsets? Gone by Christmas. When the lads say a tool's actually saving them time, I'll jump on.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **office goes first**, so we should get organised before our turn.
I'd share posts about making companies **pay for retraining**.
think: My **picking job** is all right for a few years, since jumpers are fiddly for robots.
Software planning shifts would mean **fewer hires** and more pressure on the **pick rate**.
do: Get the **forklift licence** this year instead of putting it off again.
Try the office **AI tools** once a few colleagues show they really save time.
Leave **savings** untouched and add a little more each month.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching the **tide come in** towards his spot.
S1.quote: My worry is that 'some time to adjust' turns into 'adjust by next month'.
fieldNote: He waits for **proof** from colleagues before trying tools, after failed trials like headsets.
His concern is for a **friend in scheduling** with a young son.
He moves the **forklift licence** from someday to this year: a real shift.

steps.text: Get the forklift licence this year
Try the office AI tools after colleagues prove them
Go to more union meetings about retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. And robots by 2031, so I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that it needs rules, that the government should make companies keep people on or pay them properly. I'd go to protests if the union called them. With mates I'd say: it's not the robots' fault, it's who owns them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd have about five years in the warehouse, and then I'm done there. My job's hands-on, so 2028 doesn't take it, but the planners and supervisors go, and nobody's left to promote me to. Then in 2031 the robots come for the shelves. Ama's job would hold longer, I think, so we wouldn't starve, but I'd be the one leaning on her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd cut back a bit, fewer takeaways, no new phone, and push the savings up. I'd look properly at trades that need hands in odd places, like electrician or plumber, because they'd last longer than warehouse work. I'd ask around for an apprenticeship, even if it pays less at the start. And I'd push the union to fight for redundancy money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a plan, sort of, and money in the bank, but five years isn't long to become something else when you left school at sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one leaning on Ama. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, if I'm honest. My dad was the main earner in our house and I grew up thinking that was the man's job. I know that's old-fashioned and I don't really believe it, but it would still sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrician or plumber, rather than something with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a robot fixing wiring under someone's floorboards in an old house feels further off than a robot picking a jumper off a shelf. And I'm better with my hands than with screens. I'd try AI to help me study, though, like for the theory tests.

say: I'd say the **government** must make companies keep people on or pay them properly.
I'd tell mates it's not the robots' fault, it's **who owns them**.
think: I'd have about **five years** left in the warehouse before robots take the shelves.
Ama's nursing job would hold longer, so I'd be the one **leaning on her**.
do: Cut **takeaways** and skip a new phone to push savings up.
Look for an **electrician or plumber** apprenticeship, even on lower starting pay.
Push the **union** to fight for proper **redundancy money**.
feel: **Anxious**, with money saved but little time to become **something else**.
A **sting of pride** at the thought of relying on his girlfriend.
S2.quote: A robot fixing wiring under someone's floorboards in an old house feels further off than a robot picking a jumper off a shelf.
fieldNote: He maps the **three-year robot gap** carefully: promotions vanish first, then the shelves.
He chooses **trades** in messy places as the last to be automated.
An honest admission of **old-fashioned pride** he says he doesn't really believe in.

steps.text: Cut takeaways and skip the new phone to boost savings
Apply for an electrician or plumber apprenticeship within the year
Push the union for proper redundancy pay deals
Use AI to help study for the trade theory tests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then 2034 for robots. That's seven or eight years for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message really, that companies need to share it out. But I'd say it with a bit more 'let's plan' and less shouting. I'd probably post about free training courses, because there'd be time to do them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think this is enough time to do it properly. An apprenticeship is three or four years, so I'd be qualified before the robots get to the shelves. But I'd still be watching every year, because 'a few years to see it coming' can feel like a lot until it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrician apprenticeship within a year, probably at the college on Tuesday nights first to get the maths up. I'd keep working days at the warehouse while I could. And I'd keep the savings as a cushion for when apprentice pay is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but in a busy way. Like before an exam you've actually revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said 'next year' about courses. What makes this different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date. When it's vague, I put it off. When someone says 2034, I can count backwards and see I've got to start now. That's just how my head works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five-a-side on Tuesdays, for starters, because that's when the college runs the evening class. And probably the holiday Ama and I were saving for. She'd moan but she'd get it.

say: I'd say companies must **share it out**, with more planning and less shouting.
I'd post about **free training** courses, since there'd be time to finish them.
think: An apprenticeship takes **three or four years**, so I'd qualify before robots reach the shelves.
I'd still **watch every year**, because a few years can vanish quickly.
do: Start a **maths evening class** at the college on Tuesdays within a year.
Begin an **electrician apprenticeship** while working warehouse **days**.
Keep **savings** as a cushion for low apprentice pay.
feel: **Anxious** but **busy**, like before an exam he's revised for.
S3.quote: When someone says 2034, I can count backwards and see I've got to start now.
fieldNote: A clear **date** turns his procrastination into action.
He'd sacrifice **football** and a holiday, small but real costs.
He still counts it as his **job ending**, so the worry stays.

steps.text: Enrol in the Tuesday night maths class at the college
Skip this year's holiday to protect savings for apprentice pay
Keep working warehouse days while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and then 2039 for robots. I'd be pushing 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: right, no excuses, everyone's got time to get ready, including the government. I'd tell the younger lads to pick a trade now. I'd still back the union pushing for training money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm probably fine. Twelve years is a whole career for some people. I might even get to team leader in that time, if I get quicker. The danger is that I relax and do nothing for eight years, which is very me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence first, because it's quick money. Then maybe start an electrician course in two or three years, once I've seen whether other people are actually getting work from it. And I'd keep saving, maybe put some in a pension properly, since I'd have time to grow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not worried about next year, but I'd know the end of my job is out there somewhere. It's a background hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You admitted you might relax and do nothing. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama, honestly. She'd keep at me. And maybe if I write down a date on the calendar, like 'start course by 2028', and tell the lads, so they'd take the mick if I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ama plan anything differently, family-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids in a few years. With ten years' warning I wouldn't change that. In the fast one, I'd want to wait. That's probably the biggest difference between the pictures for us.

say: I'd say everyone, including the **government**, has **no excuse** not to get ready.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **pick a trade** now.
think: **Twelve years** is a whole career for some people, so I'm probably fine.
The real danger is that I **relax** and do nothing for **eight years**.
do: Take the **forklift licence** first, because it's quick extra money.
Start an **electrician course** in two or three years, once others prove it works.
Put some savings into a **pension** so it has time to grow.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a **background hum** about his job ending someday.
S4.quote: The danger is that I relax and do nothing for eight years, which is very me.
fieldNote: He knows his own **habit of delay** and plans to use his partner and mates to beat it.
Timing changes his **family plans**: children stay on track with ten years.
His **steady** style shows: he'd wait for proof before starting the course.

steps.text: Take the forklift licence for quick extra hourly pay
Start paying a set amount into a personal pension
Keep plans to start a family in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. It's the speed, not the end point. What would help is someone paying apprentices a proper wage, so people like me can switch without burning through all our savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about pride. A lot of the lads I work with would rather do a job they hate than admit they need help or retraining. That's going to matter more than the technology, I reckon.

headlineQuote: A lot of the lads I work with would rather do a job they hate than admit they need help or retraining.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old picker** at an online clothes shop's warehouse, living with Ama, a children's nurse.
He has about **eight months saved** and uses chatbots now and then, but waits for **proof** before new tools.
He is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy about **office jobs** shrinking first.
Faster AGI pushes him towards an **electrician apprenticeship**, and he admits leaning on Ama would hurt his pride.
His biggest enemy is his own **delay**; a clear date makes him act.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the speed leaves too little time to switch trades.
whatWouldHelp: **Proper apprentice wages**, so switching doesn't burn through his savings.
